TTN is highly likely in term or late-preterm infants with tachypnea, grunting, and mild retractions; it reflects delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid and typically peaks at 2–4 hours. RDS is also very plausible—especially if preterm—but can occur in near-term infants with surfactant immaturity; onset within hours is typical. MAS is strongly considered if meconium-stained amniotic fluid was present and the infant shows signs of airway obstruction, hypoxemia, and barrel chest; onset is often immediate but may evolve over the first few hours. Early-onset sepsis must be included given its nonspecific presentation (tachypnea, lethargy, temperature instability) and potential for rapid deterioration; onset at 2 hours falls within the typical 0–72 hour window. Pneumothorax is less common but critical to recognize—it may present acutely with asymmetric chest expansion, decreased breath sounds, and sudden decompensation; spontaneous or secondary to resuscitation/PPV. Less likely diagnoses (e.g., congenital heart disease, diaphragmatic hernia, metabolic disorders) are excluded here due to later onset timing or associated features not yet reported."}

CHAOS—caused by upper airway obstruction (e.g., laryngeal atresia)—leads to hyperinflated, echogenic lungs on prenatal US and respiratory failure shortly after birth; though rare, timing aligns (0.71). {"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Congenital Central Hypoventilation Syndrome (CCHS)", "confidence": 0.85}, {"diagnosis": "Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH)", "confidence": 0.82}, {"diagnosis": "Alveolar Capillary Dysplasia with Misalignment of Pulmonary Veins (ACD/MPV)", "confidence": 0.78}, {"diagnosis": "Surfactant Protein B Deficiency", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Pierre Robin Sequence with Upper Airway Obstruction", "confidence": 0.68}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 1.602, "reasoning": "Respiratory distress beginning at 2 hours of life—after initial stabilization—rules out transient tachypnea of the newborn (typically peaks at 2–4 h but resolves by 24–48 h) and early-onset sepsis (which usually presents earlier or with systemic signs). The absence of specified infection or common pulmonary disease prompts consideration of structural, neuromuscular, or genetic disorders. CCHS is highly plausible given its hallmark onset in the first hours of life with hypoventilation disproportionate to work of breathing, often without cyanosis initially; it is frequently missed on routine imaging and requires polysomnography or PHOX2B testing. CDH remains high-probability due to its classic presentation of severe respiratory distress within hours of birth, asymmetric chest, scaphoid abdomen, and bowel sounds in the chest—though it may be subtle on initial exam if herniation is small or delayed. ACD/MPV is a lethal developmental lung disorder presenting with persistent pulmonary hypertension and refractory hypoxemia starting in the first hours; it is often misdiagnosed as PPHN or MAS until autopsy or genetic testing (FOXF1 variants). Surfactant Protein B Deficiency causes progressive respiratory failure starting within hours, unresponsive to surfactant replacement, and shows characteristic ground-glass opacities on CXR—distinct from SP-C or ABCA3 deficiencies which often present later. Pierre Robin Sequence is included because upper airway obstruction (glossoptosis, micrognathia) can manifest as apparent respiratory distress shortly after birth when tone decreases post-delivery, especially if not recognized during delivery; it is readily assessable clinically but may be overlooked without careful airway exam. Confidence scores reflect prevalence, temporal pattern specificity, and diagnostic discriminability given limited data—lower confidence for Pierre Robin reflects its relative clinical detectability and lower mortality compared to the others."}
